# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
======
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

## Two layers of code

The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.

The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.

The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:

- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.

An edit makes stale what was built from it:

- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.

# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

A generic function passed as a value takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it: a parameter, a local variable declared with the type, or an assignment. So `app(half, v)` runs for `half[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): Vector[\RR64,n\]` and `app(f: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\], v: Vector[\RR64,3\])`. Where no arrow type receives it, or the arrow type leaves a static parameter open, the value stays generic. Walk then infers the static arguments at each application. The checker refuses such a program, so do not rely on this in a program for both paths (ledger row 1021). Walk departs from this in three cases:

- An immutable top-level variable of arrow type, an object's field of arrow type and a declared arrow return type keep the generic value. So for a top-level `g: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\] = half`, `g(w)` runs for a `w: Vector[\RR64,2\]` (ledger rows 1019, 1036).
- For `appT[\T\](f: T -> T, x: T)`, `appT(half, v)` is refused, 'Unification error': `v` fixes `T` by its run-time type. Write the static argument, as `appT(half[\3\], v)` (ledger row 1018).
- A generic function declared inside a block stops at its declaration, whether it is passed or not: 'Missing type T' (ledger row 1020). Declare it at the top level.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.

- The right side of a top-level tuple binding runs once for each name and once more: `(first, second) = pairOnce()` runs `pairOnce` three times (ledger row 1026). Bind the call to one name, as `pair = pairOnce()`, then write `(first, second) = pair`.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.

In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method: a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own.

A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the list above: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- The binding is in a method of a type whose `self` walk does not carry, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the list above, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

The check has two gaps:

- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `JavaBufferedWriter` loads. A call of its inherited native method then stops with 'No Java FortressBufferedWriter carries' and the object's name (ledger row 928). Extend `WriteStream`, the library's trait of an output stream (`Library/Stream.fsi`), instead.

A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. A `||` of string literals folds into one literal, a `FlatString`, so a test that needs a `CatString` joins a literal with a variable. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `ZZ32.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/ZZ32.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
## The Bash tool and waits

The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).

- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.

## Long commands

If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:

    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &

Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.

The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.

The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.

Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.

    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
        done
        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
    }

If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.

- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.

## Stopping processes

Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.

Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.

## After an interrupt or a stop of the process

If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:

content.content:
\section{Aggregate Expressions}
\seclabel{aggregate-expr}

\note{Some operators and matrix unpasting are not yet supported.}

\note{\EXP{\mapsto} is a special syntax only in two contexts:
map aggregates and map comprehensions. (02/12/09)
}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Primary}
&::=& \emph{LeftEncloser} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \option{\emph{ExprList}} \emph{RightEncloser} \\

\emph{ExprList} &::=& \emph{Expr}(\EXP{,} \emph{Expr})$^*$ \\

\emph{ArrayExpr} &::=& \texttt{[} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \emph{RectElements} \texttt{]}\\

\emph{RectElements} &::=& \emph{Expr} \emph{MultiDimCons}$^*$\\

\emph{MultiDimCons} &::=& \emph{RectSeparator} \emph{Expr}\\

\emph{RectSeparator} &::=& \EXP{;}+\\
&$|$& \emph{Whitespace}\\

\emph{MapExpr} &::=& \{ \option{\emph{StaticArgs}} \option{\emph{EntryList}} \}\\
\end{Grammar}

\emph{Aggregate expressions} evaluate to values that are themselves
homogeneous collections of values.  Each subexpression of an aggregate
expression is evaluated in parallel in a separate implicit thread (see
\secref{threads-parallelism}).
With the exception of array expressions, the resulting
values are passed to the appropriate bracketing operator, which is a
function with a varargs parameter constructing the aggregate.
The array aggregate operations
construct the aggregate directly, after all
subexpressions have completed normally.  Any aggregate expression may
reserve storage for its result before its elements complete
evaluation.

Functions defining aggregate expressions are provided in \library\
for sets, maps, lists, matrices, vectors, and arrays.

----
\subsection{Array Expressions}
\seclabel{array-expr}

Array element expressions are enclosed in brackets. Element expressions
along a row are separated only by whitespace.
Two dimensional array expressions are written by separating rows with
newlines or semicolons.  If a semicolon appears, whitespace before
and after the semicolon is ignored.
The parts of higher-dimensional array expressions are separated
by repeated-semicolons, where the dimensionality
of the result is equal to one plus the number
of repeated semicolons.
The type of a $k$-dimensional array expression is
\EXP{\TYP{Array}k\llbracket{}T, 0, n_{\mathrm{0}}, \cdots,
         0, n_{k-1}\rrbracket},
where \VAR{T} is the union type of the types of the element expressions and
$n_0, ..., n_{k-1}$
are the sizes of the array in each dimension\footnote{
As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides \EXP{\TYP{Array}k} types for
$1 \le k \le 3$.}. This type can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T [n_{\mathrm{0}}, \cdots, n_{k-1}]}.




A $k$-dimensional array \VAR{A} is indexed by placing a sequence of
$k$ indices enclosed in brackets, and separated by commas, after an expression
evaluating to \VAR{A}.
Thus, the index is rendered as a subscript.
By default, arrays are indexed from 0.  The
horizontal dimension of an array is the last dimension mentioned in the
array index.  For example:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Expr.Array.a.tex}
then \EXP{A_{1,0}} evaluates to \EXP{4}.

An array of two
\marginnote{two or more -- Jan: I continue to disbelieve.}
dimensions whose elements are a subtype of \TYP{Number}
is a matrix.
\marginnote{
can be coerced to a matrix.
Matrix types are written
\EXP{\TYP{Matrix}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket [n_{\mathrm{0}} \times \ldots \times n_{k-1}]},
where $k > 1$.
A type of this form can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T^{n_0 \times \ldots \times n_{k-1}}}.}
Matrices are indexed in the same manner as arrays.

A one-dimensional array whose elements are a subtype of \TYP{Number}
is a vector.
\marginnote{
can be coerced to a vector.
Vector types are written \EXP{\TYP{Vector}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket [n]}.
A type of this form can be abbreviated as
\EXP{T^{n}}, unless \VAR{T} is declared in the enclosing scope
to be a physical dimension or unit.

Matrices occurring inside a matrix literal on the same row are
pasted along dimension 0. Each row is pasted along dimension 1 and the
resulting matrix is ``flattened''.  This works because matrices never
contain other matrices as elements.
}

The element expressions in an array expression may be either scalars or
array expressions themselves.  If an element is an array expression,
it is ``flattened'' (pasted) into the enclosing expression.
This pasting works because array expressions never
contain other arrays as elements.  The elements along
a row (or column) must have the same number of columns (or rows),
though two elements in different rows (columns) need not have the
same number of columns (rows).
See \secref{unpasting} for a discussion of matrix unpasting.

\chapter{Static Parameters}
\chaplabel{trait-parameters}

\note{Of the non-type static parameters, \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters are
supported by the interpreter and the compiled path, and so are static
expressions in a size, as far as \secref{static-expr} notes; the compiled type
checker does not infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit} static argument.

The examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter.}

Trait, object, and functional declarations may be
parameterized with \emph{static parameters}.
Static parameters are \emph{static variables} listed in white
square brackets \EXP{\llbracket} and \EXP{\rrbracket}
immediately after the name of a trait, object, or functional and
they are in scope of the entire body of the declaration.
Static parameters may be instantiated with static expressions discussed in
\secref{static-expr}.
In this chapter, we describe the forms that
these static parameters can take.

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{StaticParams} &::=&
\bTPl \emph{StaticParamList}\bTPr\\
\emph{StaticParamList} &::=& \emph{StaticParam}(\EXP{,} \emph{StaticParam})$^*$\\
\end{Grammar}

\section{Nat and Int Parameters}
\seclabel{natparams}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{StaticParam} &::=& \KWD{nat} \emph{Id} \\
&$|$& \KWD{int} \emph{Id} \\
\end{Grammar}

Static parameters may include one or more
\KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
Syntactically, a \KWD{nat} parameter consists of
\KWD{nat} followed by an identifier.
An \KWD{int} parameter consists of
\KWD{int} followed by an identifier.
These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values.
A \KWD{nat} parameter may be used to instantiate other
\KWD{nat} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can appear,
except that it cannot be assigned to.
An \KWD{int} parameter may be used to instantiate other
\KWD{int} parameters, or to appear in any context that a
variable of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} can appear,
except that it cannot be assigned to.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The revival decided on 28~September 2026 that a
\KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral
does (\secref{revival-inference}), and on 8~November 2026 that a \KWD{nat} or
\KWD{int} parameter used as a value is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, as a numeral
without a radix point is where nothing fixes its type and its value fits
(\secref{literals}).
This contradicts the sentence above on a \KWD{nat} parameter, which stands:
used as a value, it is not accepted where only an \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} is, as by
a variable declared of type \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, since \EXP{\mathbb{N}32}
declares no coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
The revival decided on 9~November 2026 that the four numbers of a numeral
type (\secref{literals}) are \KWD{nat} parameters of any size, which, read as
values in the body of a coercion from that type, are integers of type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}: the bound of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter to the range
of \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, which the compiled type checker
enforces, is this implementation's bound for sizes, such as the length of an
array, and not a bound of these four numbers.}
An argument whose type is a trait whose \KWD{comprises} clause lists a type at a
\KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} \KWD{where}-clause variable (\secref{trait-decls}),
passed where that listed type is expected
with a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter in the variable's place,
instantiates that parameter, for that call, with the size of the value itself,
a size known to equal only itself:
where
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{NatParam}\;\KWD{comprises}\;\{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket\}\;\KWD{where}\;\llbracket\KWD{nat}\;n\rrbracket}
is declared, a \TYP{NatParam} passed to
\EXP{f\llbracket\KWD{nat}\;m\rrbracket(x\COLON N\llbracket{}m\rrbracket)}
instantiates \VAR{m} with the size of the \VAR{N} that it is.
\revision{revival-comprises}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say how
a size known only at run time reaches a \KWD{nat} parameter.
The sentence above states the rule of the team's comment on the trait
\TYP{NatParam} of \library: ``within that function n becomes a static nat
parameter''.}

For example, the following function \VAR{makeVector}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/StatParam.Nat.tex}
declares a \KWD{nat} parameter \EXP{s_{0}}, which appears in both the parameter
type and return type of \VAR{makeVector}.

end

(************************************************************
* \subsection*{Array support}
************************************************************)

trait HasRank extends Equality[\HasRank\] excludes { Number, AnyMaybe }
  (** not yet: ``% comprises Array[\T,E,I\] where [\T,E,I\]{ T extends Array[\T,E,I\] }%'' *)
  abstract rank():ZZ32
  opr =(self, other:HasRank): Boolean
end

(* Declared Rank-n-ness *)
trait Rank[\ nat n \] extends HasRank
  rank():ZZ32
end

(** Potemkin exclusion traits.  Really we just want to say that
    ``%Rank[\n\] excludes Rank[\m\] where { m =/= n }%'', but we cannot yet. *)

trait Rank1 extends { Rank[\1\]} excludes { Rank2, Rank3, Number, String }
end

trait Rank2 extends { Rank[\2\]} excludes { Rank3, Number, String }
end

trait Rank3 extends { Rank[\3\]} excludes { Number, String }
end

(** The trait %Indexed_i[\n\]%
   indicates that something has an $i^{th}$ dimension of size $n$.  In
   general, anything which extends %Indexed_i% must also
   extend %Indexed_j% for $j < i$. *)

trait Indexed1[\ nat n \] extends HasRank end

trait Indexed2[\ nat n \] extends HasRank end

trait Indexed3[\ nat n \] extends HasRank end

(** %Index% is the type of what a subscript takes, apart from the ranges,
    which exclude it: %ZZ32%, and every tuple type whose element types are
    all %Index% types.  It extends %Any%, not %Object%, so a tuple of
    indices is an %Index% and no %Object%. **)
trait Index extends Any end

(** The indexed trait indicates that an object of type %T% can be
indexed using type %I% to obtain elements with type %E%.

An object %i% that is an instance of %Indexed% defines three basic things:

  The indexing operator %opr []%, which must be defined for every instance of
    the type.

  A suite of generators: %i.indices% generates the index space of the
    array.  %i% itself generates the values contained at those indices.
    %i.indexValuePairs% yields pairs of %(index,val)%.  All of these
    share the same natural order.  It is necessary to define one of
    %indices()% and %indexValuePairs()%, in addition to %generate()% (but
    the latter requirement can be dispensed by instead extending
    %DelegatedIndexed%).

  A set of utility functions, %assign%, %fill%, and %copy%.  Only %fill% and
    %copy% need to be defined.
**)
trait Indexed[\E, I extends Index\] extends Generator[\E\]
    (** %isEmpty()% indicates whether there are any valid indices.  It is
        defined as %|self| = 0%. *)
    getter isEmpty(): Boolean
    getter nonEmpty(): Boolean
    (** %size()% is deprecated; use %|self|% instead. *)
    abstract getter size(): ZZ32
    (** %bounds()% yields a range of indices that are valid for the
        indexed generator. *)
    abstract getter bounds(): CompactFullRange[\I\]
    (** %indexValuePairs()% generates the elements of the indexed object
        (exactly those elements that are generated by the object itself),
        but each element is paired with its index.  When we obtain
        %(i,v)% from %indexValuePairs()% we know that:
        \begin{itemize}
           \item %self[i] = v%
           \item the %i% are distinct and %i IN bounds()%
           \item stripping away the %i% yields exactly the results of %v <- self%
        \end{itemize}
        This generator attempts to follow the structure of the
        underlying object as closely as possible.  *)

type %T%, and whose lowest index is %b0%.

    The natural order of all generators is from %b0% to
    %b0+s0-1%. **)
trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]
        extends { Indexed1[\s0\], Rank1, ReadableArray[\T,ZZ32\] }
        comprises { ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\], Array1[\T,b0,s0\] }
    getter size():ZZ32
    getter bounds():CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]
    abstract getter mutability():String
    opr |self| : ZZ32

    abstract subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m: ZZ32): ReadableArray1[\T, b, s\]

    (** Offset converts from %b0%-indexing to 0-indexing,
        bounds checking en route. *)
    offset(i:ZZ32):ZZ32
    toIndex(i:ZZ32):ZZ32

    zeroIndices(): CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]
end

trait ImmutableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]
    extends { StandardImmutableArrayType[\ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\],T,ZZ32\],
              ImmutableArray[\T,ZZ32\], ReadableArray1[\T,b0,s0\] }
    getter mutability():String
    shift(o:ZZ32): ImmutableArray[\T,ZZ32\]
    opr[r: Range[\ZZ32\]] : ImmutableArray[\T,ZZ32\]
    opr[_:TrivialOpenRange] : ImmutableArray1[\T,0,s0\]

    (** %subarray% selects a subarray of this array based on static parameters.
        %b#s% are the new bounds of the array; %o% is
        the index of the subarray within the current array. **)
    subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m:ZZ32):ImmutableArray1[\T, b, s\]

    (** The %replica% method returns a replica of the array (similar layout
        etc.) but with a different element type. *)
    replica[\U\]():ImmutableArray1[\U,b0,s0\]

    copy():ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\]
    fill(v:T):ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\]
    tabulate(f:ZZ32->T):ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\]

    thaw():Array1[\T,b0,s0\]
    map[\R\](f:T->R): ImmutableArray1[\R,b0,s0\]
    ivmap[\R\](f:(ZZ32,T)->R): ImmutableArray1[\R,b0,s0\]
end

(** %Array1[\T,b0,s0\]% is a 1-dimension array whose %s0% elements are of
    type %T%, and whose lowest index is %b0%. **)
trait Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]
    extends { ReadableArray1[\T,b0,s0\],
              StandardMutableArrayType[\Array1[\T,b0,s0\],T,ZZ32\] }
    excludes {Number, String}

    getter mutability():String

    shift(o:ZZ32): Array[\T,ZZ32\]

    opr[r: Range[\ZZ32\]] : Array[\T,ZZ32\]
    opr[_:TrivialOpenRange] : Array1[\T,0,s0\]

    subarray[\nat b, nat s, nat o\](m:ZZ32):Array1[\T, b, s\]

    replica[\U\]():Array1[\U,b0,s0\]

    copy():Array1[\T,b0,s0\]
    freeze():ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\]
    map[\R\](f:T->R): Array1[\R,b0,s0\]
    ivmap[\R\](f:(ZZ32,T)->R): Array1[\R,b0,s0\]
end

trait AnyVector end

trait Vector[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat s0\]
        extends { AnyVector, Array1[\T,0,s0\], AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] }
        excludes { AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    opr +(self, v:Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
    opr -(self, v:Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
    opr -(self): Vector[\T,s0\]
    scale(t: T): Vector[\T,s0\]
    pmul(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): Vector[\T,s0\]
    dot(v: Vector[\T,s0\]): T
    fill(v:T):Vector[\T,s0\]
    tabulate(f:ZZ32->T):Vector[\T,s0\]
end

(** %__builtinFactory1% must be a non-overloaded 0-parameter factory for
   1-D arrays.  The type parameters are enshrined in \texttt{LHSEvaluator.java}
   and \texttt{NonPrimitive.java}; the factory name is enshrined in
   \texttt{WellKnownNames.java}.  There must be some factory, named in this
   file, with this type signature.  A similar thing is true for
   $k$-dimensional array types. *)
__builtinFactory1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]():Array1[\T,b0,s0\]

(** %__immutableFactory1% is a non-overloaded 0-parameter factory for
   0-indexed 1-D write-once arrays.  It is also mentioned in \texttt{WellKnownNames} as it
   is used to allocate storage for varargs. *)
__immutableFactory1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]():ImmutableArray1[\T,b0,s0\]

array1[\T, nat s0\]():Array1[\T,0,s0\]

<!-- A rehearsal of the switch-over by brute force, 2026-11-10, by a Fable worker for the review of PLAN's phases 4 and 5: a scratch tree's compiled path switched onto the interpreter's library, the library's components compiled to bytecode with every wall hacked past, and programs run against them, with each wall in the order met, its ledger row or the lack of one, the hack that passed it and what a real repair needs; run in a worktree of the worker's own, `/home/user/fortress-switch`, seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) and removed after; nothing here lands, and the scratch tree's whole diff is `switch-rehearsal.patch` beside this report. -->

# The switch-over rehearsed by brute force

The question: what stands between today's tree (`832f7d0d91`) and a program that compiles to bytecode and runs against the interpreter's library (P-37, P-33)? The method: switch a scratch tree's compiled path onto that library by the smallest change, then push, hacking past each wall, and record the walls in the order met. A hack is marked as one in the patch (`SWITCH HACK`), and the patch is not a design.

Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.30GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. Other sessions share the machine.

How the runs were made: the edited Java and Scala classes compiled into a scratch folder put first on the class path (the `fortress-repo` skill's `compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), with a private caches folder that started empty; one `ant compileAll` after the run-time classes changed.

## 1. The switch itself

The two worlds are chosen in one place for each command: `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` and `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java:373-388`), which point `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at a prelude and set the desugaring switches. The smallest change that switches the compiled path is two lines of `useCompilerLibraries()`:

    -        WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries();
    -        Types.useCompilerLibraries();
    +        WellKnownNames.useFortressLibraries();
    +        Types.useFortressLibraries();

The desugaring switches stay the compile command's. With that alone, `fortress compile Hello.fss` (one `println` of a string) passes every phase, the checker and the code generator among them, in 16 s, and writes `Hello.jar`. The program's own compile needs nothing else. Everything below is what its run needs: the library as bytecode.

## 2. The walls, in the order met

Each wall has: what fails, its kind and count, the ledger row that holds it or "no row", the hack, and what a real repair needs.

`NamingCzar.extendsClauseToInterfaces` (`NamingCzar.java:799-824`) names each parent by `jvmTypeDesc`, which answers a carried type's carrier class, so `Float extends RR64` became an interface that extends the class `FRR64`. In the prelude nothing extends a carried trait in Fortress source. Hack: a carried type in an `extends` clause is named by its own interface. This wall was met only because W13's hack made `Float` a trait below `RR64`; an object below a carried trait takes the same path. Part of the carrier design.

### W15. An array of rank 2: an abstract method over an index type that is a tuple has no implementation (row 832's kind)

    Caused by: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class fortress.FortressLibrary$__DefaultMatrix⟦FRR64,3,4⟧ does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧ offset(Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧)' of interface fortress.FortressLibrary$ReadableArray⟦FRR64,Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧
        at ...Array⟦FRR64,Tuple⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧⟧$DefaultTraitMethods._[_]:=(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2369)

`Array[\E,I\]` declares `offset(i:I): I` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2314`); `Array2` gives `offset(t1:(ZZ32,ZZ32)):(ZZ32,ZZ32)` (`:2847`). At `I = (ZZ32,ZZ32)` the abstract method takes one boxed tuple, and the body written at the tuple type was compiled with another descriptor, with no bridge between them. So `m[i,j] := x` and `m[i,j]` die on every rank-2 and rank-3 array, a `Matrix` among them. Row 832 holds the nearest shape (a generic dotted method whose single parameter has a tuple type from a tuple static argument). **No hack gets past it: it needs the code generator to emit the bridge, a rung's real work. The probe stops on this line here.**

### W16. The library's vector algebra: a generic method inherited from an api's trait has no body on the object (rows 495 and 732's kind)

    Caused by: java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class RangeInternals$CompactFullParScalarRange does not define or inherit an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract java.lang.Object map⟦…⟧(long, java.lang.String)' of interface fortress.FortressLibrary$Indexed⟦FZZ32,FZZ32⟧.
        at ...ReadableArray⟦FRR64,FZZ32⟧$DefaultTraitMethods.indexValuePairs(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2288)
        at ...FortressLibrary$fn@2716...apply(Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2716)
        at ...__bigOperator...

`a DOT b` on two `Vector[\RR64,1000\]` values reaches `Indexed`'s generic method `map[\R\]` on a range object of `RangeInternals`, which has no implementation of it: the object inherits the generic method's body from a trait of another component's api. PLAN's phase 4 names this arm ("an object's inherited generic method … dies at the generic arm", from the generic-`distribute` probe) and phase 5 names rows 495 and 496. **No hack was tried: it is the code generator's generic dotted methods, a rung's real work.** Every `map`, `ivmap` and `DOT` of microGPT's vocabulary is on it.

## 3. The code generator over the library today, against F-34

`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/codegen.sh`, the probe of F-34, run twice on the scratch tree.

On the seeded tree, unchanged: `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` and `FlatString` are refused whole at the wrappers (row 874), and the other eleven components give 11 refused declarations in 6 kinds, 185 emitted.

With W2's tables, W3's search and W4's two lines, so with every helper string as landed (F-34 put the strings back on glue classes to get past row 874): **24 refused declarations in 8 kinds, 749 emitted, no component failure**, against F-34's 38 in 10.

The probe counts a declaration at its first wall and skips the dispatch methods (`-Dprobe.skipOverloads=true`). Two differences from that count in the real compile: with `SubString` past its `label`, `String.fss` shows row 818's 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions' at `concatAndBalanceIfNecessary` (`String.fss:61`); and the real compile does generate `FortressLibrary`'s dispatch methods, in about 70 s for the component, with no refusal.

What the count cannot see: W6's 244 duplicate methods, and whatever the JVM's verifier refuses, since the probe runs no emitted class (F-34 says so).

## 4. How far each program got

The library order under the switch, each component compiled by name: `AnyType`, `FortressBuiltin` (14 s), `FortressLibrary` (73 to 79 s, 2,490 jar entries), `RangeInternals` (38 to 51 s), `NativeArray`, `FlatString`, `String`, `List`, `Stream`, `NatReflect`, `TypeProxy`, `Writer`, `CovariantCollection`, `OneShotFlag`: about 200 s, against 100 to 110 s for the prelude's five. With every hack in, 17 declarations are still left out of the jars: `assert`, `deny`, `simplestRationalBetween`, `__filter`, `__bigOperator2` and `Generator2` of `FortressLibrary`; `CatString`, `EmptyString`, `SubString`, `concatAndBalanceIfNecessary` and `stringifyChars` of `String`; `ArrayList`, `app`, `List` and `<|_|>` of `List`; `APPCOV`; `OneShot`.

`fortress link Hello.fss` under the switch exits 0 with no message in 4.6 s; linking met no wall. Row 320 (an api implemented by a component of another name) was not met: each of the fourteen components exports the api of its own name.

Each program below was also run under walk on the base build (`tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base32 …`), which printed the same lines as the compiled run where the compiled run ended.

| program | what it does | compiled against the one library |
|---|---|---|
| `Hello` | `println("Hello, one library")` | compiles with the switch alone; runs after W1 to W10: `Hello, one library` |
| `Arr` | `array1[\ZZ32,8\]()`, a `for` over `seq(0#8)` that writes `i i`, then `println("a[5] = " \|\| a[5].asString)` | compiles; runs after W11 and W12: `a[5] = 25` |
| `Dot` | two `Array1[\RR64,0,1000\]`, filled in a loop, then `s += a[i] b[i]` in a `seq` loop | compiles; runs after W13 and W14: `dot = 499500.0` |
| `DotLib` | the same on `Vector[\RR64,1000\]` with the library's `a DOT b` and `SUM[\RR64\][i <- 0#1000] a[i] b[i]` | compiles; dies at W16 |
| `MatVec` | `array2[\RR64,3,4\]()` written by `m[i,j] := …`, times a vector in two `seq` loops | compiles; dies at W15 at the first `m[i,j] :=` |
| `MatVecLib` | `Matrix[\RR64,3,4\]`, `Vector[\RR64,4\]`, `r = m v` | compiles; dies at W15 |
| microGPT's flat program and its quick check | `explorations/run-c4/src/` | stopped by the checker, below |

So a program with rank-1 arrays and its own loops compiles and runs against the interpreter's library. A matrix, the library's own vector algebra and microGPT do not.

### microGPT's flat program

`fortress compile` of the four components of `explorations/run-c4/src/`, copied, under the switch. Each count is a floor, since the checker stops a block at its first failing statement (row 474).

<!-- Probe Y of the plan review of 2026-11-10 (its section 7.4), run 2026-11-13 by a Fable worker: whether one build of the tree can compile and run a program against the compiler's prelude and against the interpreter's library, with the prelude's run-time value classes kept and a second, re-parented set beside them; done in a scratch worktree, `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, seeded from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base32` (`832f7d0d91`) with the rehearsal's patch applied; it works, and this note gives what ran, how the library is selected, every hack, the walls, the cost of the second set and an estimate in rungs; nothing here lands, and the scratch tree's whole diff is `probe-y.patch` beside this report. -->

# Probe Y: one build, two libraries

**The answer: yes.** One `ant compileAll` of the scratch tree gives a build that compiles and runs the one-line program against the compiler's prelude, as today, and against the interpreter's library, chosen by one environment variable at the compile and at the run. The rehearsal's `Array1` program and its dot loop also run against the interpreter's library in that build, by hand and through the test harness. A sample of the compiled tests passes against the prelude in the same build. No wall stopped the probe.

The base is `832f7d0d91`, the rehearsal's. "The rehearsal" is `switch-rehearsal.md`, beside this note; its walls are W1 to W16 and its hacks 1 to 12. "The review" is `explorations/reviews/plan-review-2026-11-10.md`. "The one library" is the interpreter's library.

Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.10GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` for the runs by hand and 4 in the harness. Another workflow ran beside the probe; the load was 0.2 at the first build and up to 9.8 later. No timing here is a pair.

## 1. What ran

All in `/home/user/fortress-probe-y`, after one `ant compileAll` (43 s, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`) and the two library orders (section 5).

The three programs are the rehearsal's by its description (its section 4); its files were not kept, so they were written again. `Hello` is `run(): () = println("Hello, one library")`.

**The prelude** (no variable set, the tree's own `default_repository/caches`):

    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
    Hello, one library                         (both exit 0)
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss
    Arr.fss:5:6-10: Array1 is undefined.       (exit 255; Dot.fss alike, 2 errors)

`Arr` and `Dot` cannot compile against the prelude in any build: it has no array type (row 305).

**The one library** (`FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/default_repository/caches-one`, and for each run the rehearsal's flags that switch the verifier off, its W7):

    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Hello.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Hello
    Hello, one library
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Arr.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Arr
    a[5] = 25
    $ ../../bin/fortress compile Dot.fss ; ../../bin/fortress run Dot
    dot = 499500.0                             (every command exit 0)

With `-verbose:class`, the prelude's run of `Hello` loads no class whose name holds `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` or `FlatStringC`, and the one library's run loads none whose name holds `CompilerBuiltin` or `CompilerLibrary` (each count 0).

**Through the harness, against the one library.** Three `.test` files (`link`, `run`, `run_out_contains=` the line above) for the three programs, in one `fortress junit` run with the same three settings:

    . run .../ArrOne (1375ms) a[5] = 25
    . run .../DotOne (1826ms) dot = 499500.0
    OK (6 tests)                               (16 s)

**Through the harness, against the prelude, in the same build** (`ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`, on `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests`):

- Twelve files chosen for what the second set touches (helpers that raise, the `NN32`, integer, `Char` and `asFloat` helper families, a caught `FileNotFoundException`, two `atomic` tests, one refusal of the code generator): `OK (22 tests)`.
- Every seventh file of the folder's sorted list, 125 files: `Tests run: 205, Failures: 4`. The four are `XXXFortToStringRungS`, `XXXGenericFunctionalMethodSelfSecond`, `XXXGenericTraitGenericFunctionalMethod` and `XXXPowNN64CompiledRungE`, each 'Could not load …: Resource not found'. The same four files run alone on the base build's code (`old-fortress.sh … junit`) fail in the same way, `Tests run: 4, Failures: 4`: a file with only a `run` step needs its sibling's jar, which a sample leaves out. So the sample shows no test that the second set disturbed.

**What did not run, and what was not tried.** The whole compiled tracks (1,907 tests) were not run against the prelude; the sample is 137 files of 876 in one folder. Walk was not run: the rehearsal's library text breaks it in a scratch tree (its hack 4), and this probe kept that text. A matrix, the library's `DOT` and microGPT stop where the rehearsal stopped (its W15, W16 and section 4); nothing here changes that. The cheaper form that the carriers' review proposes (section 7) was not tried.

## 2. How the library is selected

One variable, `FORTRESS_LIBRARY`. Unset, everything is as today. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`:

- **At the compile.** `WellKnownNames.compiledPathUsesOneLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java`) reads the variable once for the JVM (or `-Dfortress.library=one`). `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java`), which every compiled-path command calls, points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` at the one library's names where it is set, and at the prelude's where not.
- **At the run.** `bin/fortress_classpath` puts `ProjectFortress/build-one`, the second set's classes, before `ProjectFortress/build`. `bin/run_classpath` builds on that script, so the run's JVM finds the second set's `FZZ32` first. The compile's JVM gets the same class path.
- **The caches.** A caches folder holds one library's jars and the programs compiled against it, so the one library has its own: `default_repository/caches-one`, named by hand in `FORTRESS_CACHES`.

One JVM serves one library: `NamingCzar`'s tables are filled once, when the class loads, as on the base (`NamingCzar.fortLib`). The harness fits this: its `run` step is a process of its own that inherits the environment, so a test track against the one library is the same harness started with the three settings.

### 7.3 What the first compiled timing says, and what it cannot say

The timing (the rehearsal's section 5): the loop `s += a[i] b[i]` over two arrays of 1,000 `RR64`, run 5,000 times, 5 million iterations. Compiled against the one library, 1.4 s with the JVM's start; a one-line program takes 0.6 s, so about 0.8 s for the loop. Under walk, 39.8 s, about 36 s for the loop.

For the Java side, this review ran the same loop in plain Java on this machine (not in the rehearsal's run, at a load of 1.7 to 2.4): 7.2 ms for the first pass in a cold JVM, 2.5 to 6.1 ms for the next four.

**What it says.**

- Compiled code on the one library is about 45 times faster than walk on this loop.
- It is of the order of a hundred times slower than Java: 0.8 s against 7 ms cold, which is about 110 times, and more against a warm pass. Per iteration, about 160 ns against about 1 ns.
- Boxing does not explain that distance. The Java models of the compiled run time's boxes behind a generic array put boxing at about 7 times on a dot product (F-11). So a factor of 15 or more stands in what the one library and the generated code put between the loop and the array: the read through the store's native wrapper, with a check of the thread and the transaction on every access and a `cast` on every read (F-333; `reviews/parallelism-foundations-2026-11-08.md`, section 6), the sequential range's closure for each iteration, and the transaction check and the box on the accumulator (row 641). None of these has a measured share. The nearest numbers on file, from other sessions and on the prelude, are 37 ns an iteration for a scalar loop (F-12) and 31 ns an element for a loop over the prelude's vector (F-40).
- For scale: one training step of the pure-Java microGPT is 0.113 ms, about 200K multiply-adds (`java-baseline/python-comparison.md`, section 1). At 160 ns for each, the same arithmetic written as plain loops over rank-1 arrays would take about 32 ms a step, some 280 times the baseline. That is arithmetic on one timing, not a forecast: the model is not written as plain loops, and section 5.2's factor for the library's matrix product comes on top.

**What it cannot say.**

- Nothing about steady state. The compiled loop ran for 0.8 s in all, with the JIT's warm-up inside it.
- Nothing certain as a ratio. It is one run, not a pair, on a machine at a load of 3.7 to 4.8 on four CPUs.
- Nothing about unboxed numbers. Every number in it is a box; decisions A and B are not built. The verifier was off, which bears on loading, not on the loop.
- Nothing about microGPT's kernels. It is rank 1, in the program's own loop. No matrix, no view, no `mul`, no library reduction and no parallel loop ran.

So the second unknown of section 4.3 has a first, rough answer: today's distance to Java is about two orders of magnitude before the library's own algorithms are counted, and most of it is not boxing. That makes phase 6 a larger piece than its list in PLAN shows, and it is one more reason to have a compiled kernel under the gate early, where each of these costs can be measured and removed.

## 2. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** first checks a program's types with the **checker**, then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. The **switch-over** is the move of the compiled path onto the one library, after which the prelude is deleted.
- Your decision P-33 says how the switch-over's work goes: first microGPT's **slice**, the parts of the one library that microGPT needs. The **selector** lets one compile command read the one library beside the prelude. Each problem that only the one library shows is then fixed as its own small change, with its own test, under the full check.
- A **wall** is a place where the compiler or the compiled library stops.
- A **rung** is one change. One worker builds it, and a second, the skeptic, checks it. A **run** is one launch of the batch workflow. The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
- A **value object** is an object without identity: two with equal contents are the same value. No type can extend an object.
- A **payload class** is a small class written by hand in Java that holds a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. Under the chosen form, the code generator writes the class of `ZZ32` itself, on top of the payload class `FZZ32`.
- The **ledger** is the list of known defects. A **row** is one defect. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
- **microGPT** is the model program. No rung changes a line of it.

### The go

None yet. You asked on 13 November for this batch to be planned, and said that its start is not authorized. The coordinator launches nothing until you say so. Each fork below has a default. None needs your answer before the start: none bends a decision of yours, and none touches microGPT.

### The two runs

- **Run 1, climb batch 33, six rungs:** S, D, V, Q, I and C.
- **Run 2, climb batch 33b, four rungs:** N, W, G and R, on run 1's landed tree.
- **Why two runs.** N, W, G and R need S on `main` first. N's table of names follows S's selector, and the tests of W, G and R compile programs under it. A rung cannot build on another rung of its own run.
- **Why I is in run 1.** Rung N of run 2 edits the same method of the code generator. In run 1 no rung edits it.

### Run 1, rung by rung

Each program is shortened to the lines that matter.

**S. The selector.**

- What it changes: the commands. `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` makes the compile command read the one library, with a caches folder of its own. A new group of tests runs that way inside the full check.
- The program that fails today:
### The merge

- Rung S: one change of the commands, no code-generator file.
- Rungs V, Q and I edit the code generator's main file, `CodeGen.java`, in different methods. D, C and S share no file with them.
- In run 2, N, W and G edit the code generator's table of names, `NamingCzar.java`, and N, G and R edit `CodeGen.java`, each in methods of its own. None needs another rung of run 2.
- No two rungs of one run edit the same method. Rung I of run 1 and rung N of run 2 edit one method, the dotted call's code, and N is read again on I's landed code. The order and the files are in section 4, "The rule the rungs keep".

### The measures

- **Declarations of the one library that the code generator refuses** (F-34): 17, in 5 kinds, on today's code. The script prints 18: it counts one declaration twice.
  - Run 1: V should take the 4 that stop at its wall, and I the 1 of row 540, so 12, if nothing stands behind them. Behind `List`'s `ArrayList` stands a second crash, row 812's, which V also repairs. So 12 to 17.

The checker refuses its helper file `FlatArrays` first, with 17 errors of static types, the ones that F-58 counts. That work is a later phase's. This batch moves the library's side only: after run 2 a small program with an array compiles against the one library. No program can run there until the one library compiles whole, which is the batch after's work.

### For the batch after, in this order

1. The carriers, the run time's prelude names and `NN32`'s getters, above, with the first program that runs on the one library as their test.
2. `Generator2`'s third wall, and what else the measure shows then. Then the one library compiles whole, and `Hello` runs against it under the gate. Its library order of fourteen compiles joins the selector's track.
