Fortress revival · a teaching page · 17 November 2026

Arrays in Fortress

You asked how arrays work, how the rehearsal ran them with no array decision taken, and what work stands before an array program runs. This page goes from small programs up to the design. Each program on it ran under walk today, and its output is shown as it printed.

Sections

  1. The short answers
  2. An array, written and typed
  3. The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s
  4. How the sizes ride in the type
  5. Where the elements live today
  6. Boxing, and what it costs
  7. What the rehearsal ran, and why its loop was slow
  8. From here to an array program that runs
  9. Your design questions: decided, built at a default, open
  10. The deeper reports

1The short answers

  • The array program that runs first is the rehearsal’s smallest one. It makes an array of 8 ZZ32 with the library’s factory, writes i i into each element, and prints a[5] = 25. After the second run of the batch that is landing now, it compiles against the one library, the interpreter’s library. It runs only in the batch after that, once the whole library compiles to bytecode.
  • You need to do nothing now. The rehearsal ran arrays with no array decision, because an array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The compiler compiles them as it compiles any other library code. The open array decisions are about speed and about the model’s own types. They aren’t about running.
  • An array is half language, half library. The language gives the literal [1 2 3], the type shorthand ZZ32[3] and the subscript syntax. The library gives every type behind them. Array1, Vector and Matrix are in FortressLibrary, which every program sees without an import.
  • The sizes ride in the type on both paths today. Walk checks them when a line runs. The compiled checker checks them before the compile. The compiled run time carries each size as a small object and writes it into the name of each class that it makes.
  • Every element today is a boxed object, a number wrapped in a heap object. One exception exists: an immutable RR64 array over a bare double[], which the team wrote. “Nothing chooses it” means that no factory returns it. A program gets it only by naming it.
  • The rehearsal’s loop was about 100 times slower than Java. Boxing explains a factor of 6 to 7, by Java models of the boxes. The rest has no measured share. The record names four suspects.
  • Boxed numbers now change no array decision. Your decisions fix the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed. A bare-double store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box, so unboxing the reads and the arithmetic is a separate decision.
References
  1. The program and its compile after the second run: CLIMB-BATCH-33.md, section 2, “R. A method found by its interface” and “The measures”; its run in the batch after: the same file, “For the batch after, in this order”, item 4.
  2. The other points: each section below, with its own references.

2An array, written and typed

Start with the specification’s own example, and a few more lines. typecase picks the first arm whose type matches the value’s type when the program runs, like Swift’s switch with case is T.

A: ZZ32[3,3] = [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]
println("A[1,0] = " A[1,0])
println("|A| = " |A|)
v: RR64[3] = [1.0 2.0 3.0]
println("v DOT v = " (v DOT v))
typecase v of
  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("v is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\]")
  else => println("v is no vector")
end
s: String[2] = ["ab" "cd"]
typecase s of
  AnyVector => println("s is a vector")
  Array1[\String,0,2\] => println("s is an Array1[\\String,0,2\\], no vector")
  else => println("s is something else")
end

Under walk, it printed:

A[1,0] = 4
|A| = 9
v DOT v = 14.0
v is a Vector[\RR64,3\]
s is an Array1[\String,0,2\], no vector

What the lines show:

  • Elements along a row are separated by spaces. Rows are separated by a semicolon or a new line. Two semicolons separate the planes of a 3-dimensional array.
  • ZZ32[3,3] is shorthand. The specification types a literal of k dimensions as Arrayk[\T, 0, n0, ..., 0, nk-1\], and lets you write it T[n0, ..., nk-1]. So ZZ32[3,3] means Array2[\ZZ32, 0, 3, 0, 3\]: for each dimension, its lowest index, 0, and its size, 3. That is the “notation on the number type” that you saw in the opening chapters.
  • A[1,0] is row 1, column 0, counted from 0: the 4.
  • The same literal syntax gave three kinds of array. Numbers in two dimensions gave a matrix, numbers in one a Vector, which has vector arithmetic such as DOT. Strings gave a plain Array1. The specification says the context decides. The library decides it: its factory tests the element type against the eight number types.
  • The overview chapter also writes RR^3, a vector of length 3. Neither path builds that notation. Walk reads it as a type of its own, not as the library’s Vector. Today v: RR64^3 = [1.0 2.0 3.0] bound, and the println(v) after it stopped: “bug! Couldn’t figure out Matrix [\RR64\]^(3) <: Object”. Write RR64[3] or Vector[\RR64,3\].
References
  1. The literal syntax, its type and the shorthand: Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex, “Array Expressions”, lines 117 to 137; the example, SpecData/examples/basic/Expr.Array.a.fss.
  2. “Whether an array aggregate expression evaluates to an array, a vector, or a matrix is inferred from context”, and T^n: Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex, lines 735 to 773 and 934 to 938; the examples Overview.Expression.aggregate.a.fss (a:ZZ32[5] = [0 1 2 3 4]) and Overview.Moving.fss (RR^3).
  3. The factory’s test of the element type: Library/FortressLibrary.fss, lines 2842 to 2856, array1; FACTS F-229, “array1 and array2 give a vector and a matrix only at the eight number types”.
  4. T^n under walk: gap ledger row 24, “a T^n parameter type accepts no library array under walk”. The stop of the binding’s println is today’s run, a shape that the row does not name.
  5. The runs: the program above as Literal.fss, run with bin/fortress in a worktree seeded from the base build at c3b16ef2d1, whose library equals main’s at 9f2ff9b04e.

3The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

You were right twice. The literal looks built in, and it is. The types are library types, and they are too. Here is the split.

The language, its parser and walk, give:

  • the literal, [1 2 3; 4 5 6];
  • the shorthand T[n, m] for Array2[\T, 0, n, 0, m\];
  • the subscript forms a[i], a[i, j] and a[i] := v;
  • the static parameters, [\T, nat n\], where nat marks a size that the type carries.

The library gives:

  • Array[\E, I\], an array of any rank with no size in its type. I is the index type: ZZ32, or a pair (ZZ32, ZZ32) for rank 2.
  • Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\], Array2 and Array3, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
  • Vector[\T, nat s0\] and Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\], for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
  • the factories: array1[\T, n\](), vector, matrix, and array[\T\](n) for a size known only when the program runs.
  • the subscript itself. a[i] calls a library operator, opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i)), as Swift’s a[i] calls a subscript that the type declares.

The two meet at two names. Walk knows the trait Array plus the rank, and the factory __builtinFactory plus the rank. To build [1 2 3] at a declared type, walk calls __builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]() and copies the elements in. The library’s comment says the names are “enshrined” in walk. A literal with no declared type is not built into an array today.

So Array1 is not in a collections component that a program imports, as List is. It’s in FortressLibrary, the prelude of the one library. The specification notes that the library provides Array1 to Array3.

In your frames: Swift’s [Double] is shorthand for the standard library’s Array<Double>. Fortress’s RR64[3] is shorthand for the library’s Array1[\RR64,0,3\], and the size is part of the type. Scala’s Array[Double] is a special case of the Scala compiler, which makes it a JVM double[]. Fortress has no such special case yet. Which store an element type gets is one of your open questions.

References
  1. The library’s array types and factories: Library/FortressLibrary.fsi, Array and array at lines 1612 to 1637; ReadableArray1, Array1, Vector and the factories at lines 1704 to 1816; Array2 at 1851, Matrix at 1893, Array3 at 1960.
  2. The subscript operator: Library/FortressLibrary.fss, line 2384.
  3. The two names: WellKnownNames.java, lines 30 to 35; walk’s build of a literal, LHSEvaluator.java, lines 119 to 151; “enshrined”: FortressLibrary.fsi, lines 1786 to 1793.
  4. A literal with no declared type: gap ledger row 49, “an array literal with no declared type is not built into an array under walk”.
  5. The library’s note: aggregate.tex, lines 134 to 136, “As of March 2008, the Fortress library provides Arrayk types for 1 ≤ k ≤ 3.”; the prelude of the one library: POSITIONS P-37, “One library, the interpreter’s, is the library that the compiler checks”.

4How the sizes ride in the type

The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads its size from its type:

trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
    getter size(): ZZ32 = s0
    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
        r = i - b0
        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
        r
    end

|a| is s0, and the bounds check compares the index with s0. A product names a shared size once, so the shapes must match:

opr juxtaposition[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
    (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\]

An n-by-m matrix times a vector of m gives a vector of n. Here is a program that uses the sizes, with a 2-by-2 matrix to show that order matters:

len[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): ZZ32 = n

run(): () = do
  u: RR64[3] = [1.0 2.0 3.0]
  w: RR64[4] = [1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0]
  println("len(u) = " len(u) ", len(w) = " len(w))
  q: RR64[2,2] = [1.0 2.0; 3.0 4.0]
  x: RR64[2] = [1.0 1.0]
  println("q x = " (q x) ", x q = " (x q))
  m: RR64[2,3] = [1.0 0.0 2.0; 0.0 1.0 1.0]
  println("m u = " (m u))
  println("u + u = " (u + u))
  println("u + w = " (u + w))
end

Under walk, it printed (the error shortened):

len(u) = 3, len(w) = 4
q x = [0#2][ 3.0 7.0 ], x q = [0#2][ 4.0 6.0 ]
m u = [0#2][ 7.0 5.0 ]
u + u = [0#3][ 2.0 4.0 6.0 ]
Shapes.fss:16:23:
Failed to find any matching overload, args = (__DefaultVector[\RR64,3\],__DefaultVector[\RR64,4\]), ...

[0#2] means lowest index 0, 2 elements. len found n from its argument. No + takes a vector of 3 and a vector of 4, so the last line failed.

How each path carries the sizes:

  • Walk keeps them in each object’s type when the program runs: __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\], the library’s vector object at size 3. When walk makes the object, it binds each nat parameter to its number, so a body reads s0 as a value. Walk finds a mismatch only when the line runs.
  • The compiled checker checks sizes before the compile, so it refuses a call whose sizes don’t match. Two sizes are equal when they’re written alike once numerals are computed: 2 3 equals 6, but m n doesn’t equal n m. It refuses a size outside ZZ32’s range, to match the JVM’s int indices.
  • The compiled run time compiles a generic declaration once, as a template. At first use, the class loader makes the class of each instance, and the sizes become part of its name. The rehearsal’s stack trace names __DefaultMatrix⟦FRR64,3,4⟧. Inside, each size has one descriptor object, from RTTIsize.of, used in type tests when the program runs. Where a body reads s0 as a number, the loader writes in the constant, FZZ32.make(3). This is your picture of sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names. No optimization reads a size yet: a loop bounded by the size constant measured no faster than one bounded by the length read when it runs.

A size known only when the program runs comes through reflect:

make(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.5)

x = make(2 + 1)
println("x = " x)
typecase x of
  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("x is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\] when it runs")
  else => println("x has no size when it runs")
end
x = [0#3][ 0.5 0.5 0.5 ]
x is a Vector[\RR64,3\] when it runs

The declared type Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] holds no size. Inside the factory, reflect(n) turns the number into a value N[\3\] that carries it, and a generic function that takes N[\n\] binds n to 3 for that call. So the object is a sized vector when it runs. The checker reads such a size as fixed for that one call. A compiled call of this kind fails the JVM’s verification today, so it runs only under walk. microGPT’s flat program makes its arrays this way, with types that hold no size.

5Where the elements live today

A Vector[\RR64,3\] made by array1 is three objects deep:

  1. __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\], the vector, holds mem: PrimitiveArray[\RR64,3\];
  2. PrimitiveArray holds mem: JavaArrayStore, the store;
  3. the store holds the elements in Java.

A matrix of 2 by 3 holds one rank-1 store of s0 s1 cells, 6, row by row, and reads cell i s1 + j. A size can be a product.

The third object differs by path:

  • Under walk, walk answers the store with its own Java object, an AtomicArray of walk’s boxed values.
  • On the compiled path, against the one library, as in the rehearsal, the store is the Java class FortressArrayStore, an Object[] of boxed values such as FRR64 objects. Inside an atomic block, each read and write of an element goes through the transaction, keyed by the array and the index.
  • On the compiled path on main today, there is no array type at all: the compiler’s prelude has none, so a program that names Array1 gets “Array1 is undefined”.

The store over a bare double array is PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\], the team’s immutable RR64 array, in the one library’s NativeArray. Its store is a JavaRR64ArrayStore. Walk answers it with a double[], and its compiled class, FortressRR64ArrayStore, holds a double[]. It has get and init, and no put, since it’s immutable. “Nothing chooses it” means this:

im = immutableArray1[\RR64,3\]()
typecase im of
  PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the double[] store")
  PrimImmutableArray[\RR64,3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the general store")
  else => println("immutableArray1 chose something else")
end
r = PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\]()
r.init0(0, 1.5)
r.init0(1, 2.5)
r.init0(2, 0.25)
println("the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = " (r[0] + r[1] + r[2]))
immutableArray1 chose the general store
the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = 4.25

The store works, but the factory for an immutable RR64 array returns the general store. How a factory chooses each element type’s store is your first open question.

The native arrays of the compiler’s prelude are something else. The prelude is the compiled path’s own small library, which goes at the switch-over. It has ZZ32Vector, over a Java int[] in the class FZZ32Vector, and StringVector, over a String[], both written by hand by the team in August 2011. They have no type parameters and no size in their types. There’s no RR64 version. Neither is a generator, so for x <- v fails, and neither can be a type argument. Each read takes a boxed index and returns a new boxed ZZ32: the storage is unboxed, and the traffic is boxed. Your decision keeps the prelude as it is and deletes its files at the switch-over, so these two go with it.

6Boxing, and what it costs

A boxed number is a number held in a heap object. On the compiled path an RR64 is an object of the Java class FRR64, with one double field: Java’s Double against double, or a Double[] against a double[]. An unboxed number is the bare double, in a register or in a double[]. Today the code generator boxes every number, so a compiled RR64 loop holds no dadd or dmul.

What it costs, measured in Java models of the compiled run time’s boxes against double[]:

  • a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
  • a 16 by 16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
  • the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.

An Object[] behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 9 %, 1.6 % and 4.8 % on top. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t.

The JIT, HotSpot’s C2, removes a temporary box in a hot loop when the box doesn’t escape. One box stays for each assignment to a mutable variable in each iteration, 24 bytes for an RR64. That was observed once. An array element escapes, since it’s stored, so its box stays.

A double[] store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a double[] read and written through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 times for boxed storage. So storage and traffic are two problems. Where the elements live is the store’s question. Where the reads and the arithmetic run unboxed is a separate decision.

“We go with boxed numbers now” means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, so that compiled code can later hold a ZZ32 as a bare int. The second run’s number rung writes each number type’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value. Code still passes boxes until the unboxing decision is built, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.

For arrays it changes no decision. Your decision already fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and the sizes in the types now, not first as run-time fields. Your words of 8 November: “All numerical code in HPC settings must eventually run unboxed in the compiled path. All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.” The store in a field is the seam: a factory can later put a double[] store under Vector[\RR64,n\] without changing the traits or a program.

7What the rehearsal ran, and why its loop was slow

The switch-over rehearsal of 10 November worked in a scratch tree, a throwaway copy where nothing lands. Two lines pointed its compiled path at the one library. Twelve marked hacks got it past each wall. The one library’s 14 components compiled to bytecode in about 200 s. Then:

  • a one-line program printed Hello, one library;
  • the array program printed a[5] = 25;
  • a dot product in the program’s own loop printed dot = 499500.0;
  • the library’s DOT and a matrix died at two walls of the code generator, both fixed since;
  • microGPT’s flat program stopped at the checker, 17 errors, most of them its arrays without sizes.

Probe Y, on 13 November, ran the same programs in one build that serves either library by one setting. The batch now landing puts that setting on main: FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one makes the compile command read the one library.

The dot program, as rewritten from the rehearsal’s description:

a: Array1[\RR64,0,1000\] = array1[\RR64,1000\]()
b: Array1[\RR64,0,1000\] = array1[\RR64,1000\]()
for i <- seq(0#1000) do
  a[i] := asFloat(i)
  b[i] := 1.0
end
var s: RR64 = 0.0
for i <- seq(0#1000) do s += a[i] b[i] end
println("dot = " || s.asString)

Under walk today, it and the array program printed the compiled runs’ lines, dot = 499500.0 and a[5] = 25.

The rehearsal timed that loop run 5K times, 5M iterations. Compiled, the whole process took 1.4 s, about 0.8 s for the loop. Under walk, 39.8 s, about 36 s for the loop. Java over double[] takes 7.5 ms in a cold JVM and 4.4 ms warm. So it’s about 160 ns an iteration against about 1 ns, of the order of 100 times. That’s one run each, in different sessions at different loads, with the JIT’s warm-up inside the 0.8 s and the JVM’s verifier off. It’s an order of magnitude, no more.

Why so slow, if boxing is 6 to 7 times? Boxing explains that much, by the Java models. The rest has no measured share. By reading the code, one read a[i] goes:

  1. to the subscript operator, which calls offset(i), with its bounds check against s0;
  2. to the vector’s get, then PrimitiveArray’s get, which casts the element to RR64 with a type test;
  3. to the store’s get, through a generated wrapper, to a Java helper;
  4. to FortressArrayStore.get, which checks whether the thread runs a transaction, then reads the element as a volatile read, as for a variable that another thread may write.

The record names four suspects for the rest:

  • those layers of the read, with their checks and the cast;
  • the range seq(0#1000), which calls a closure for each iteration;
  • the check for a transaction before every read and write of the mutable s, outside atomic too, 1 to 2 ns a check, which another probe measured at 64 % of a loop over an array with mutable variables;
  • the new box for s in each iteration.

Read the number as you’d read a timing from a Swift debug build. It shows that the code runs, and how far it is from the goal. It doesn’t show what the code will cost. A profile that splits the time is proposed in the plan, not run.

8From here to an array program that runs

Three words first. A rung is one change, which one worker builds and a second checks. A run is one launch of a batch’s rungs. The gate is the full check before a run lands.

Run 1 of climb batch 33, landing now. For arrays, its step is the setting: FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one makes the compile command read the one library. A println program and a QQ binding then compile. Neither runs, since the one library has no bytecode yet. A program that names Array1 still stops: “Not in the trait table: Array1”.

Run 2, next, on your same go.

After it, five programs compile against the one library, the array program among them. None runs.

The batch after, in its planned order:

  1. The carriers: a Java class for the one library for each built-in type that a hand-written class carries when the program runs, the two array stores among them. Also the 105 exception names in the run time that name the prelude, and two getters of NN32.

9Your design questions: decided, built at a default, open

Do you need to do something now? No. No fork of the batch touches the array design, and the array program runs without it. One choice for the batch after is on your review list, near this path: whether the compiler may skip a declaration that it refuses, so that programs run sooner, as the rehearsal did. The coordinator’s default is no skipping mode: the one library is compiled only when it compiles whole.

Decided by you, each built or binding:

  • Unboxed doubles, and arrays of them, are required.
  • Each number type’s array is stored unboxed in a Java array of its primitive type, RR64’s double[] first. Every array gets the most efficient store that its element type allows. Sizes stay in the types as nat parameters, which the checker checks. A first version with the sizes only as run-time fields was rejected.
  • Sizes are checked, and a size outside ZZ32’s range is refused. A size travels at run time as a descriptor object. A size may hold arithmetic, compared by its written form. All three are built.
  • The model’s text is the notation. Any change to a model line comes to you as a diff.
  • +, - and MAX between an array and a number come from the library. The diagonal matrix keeps its own fast product.
  • fill takes a value, and tabulate a function. An array’s index type is bounded by Index.
  • The store sits in a field and its helpers run on both paths. The compiled store is an Object[], tracked by element in a transaction. That’s built.
  • Each built-in number type is one value object.

Built at a default, waiting for your answer:

  • The element bound of Vector and Matrix, T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }: a number that is a ring at its own type. The question is one bound for the whole family, or one per operation.
  • A size known only at run time: the checker reads it as fixed for that call, by the team’s own commented clause, NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\].

Open, with no default. They come back after the switch-over, in the phase in which microGPT compiles. The record names three of them by letters.

  • How the array factory chooses the store of each element type.
  • Whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type.
  • Whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized Array[\E,I\].
  • Decision A: how an array of a number type, made through the generic array traits, gets its unboxed store. The ways on file:
    • A1, the library’s own test of the element type in the generic factories, as array1 already picks a vector, with the store returned through cast. It was checked and run on both paths in a probe.
    • A2, a plain RR64 factory beside the generic one, chosen by dispatch. Walk refuses the pair at load today.
    • A3, a factory name for each element type.
    • A4, the class loader makes a different class for an RR64 instance, with a double[] field. That’s the team’s direction. Nothing of it is built or measured. On 20 September you wrote: “I would try to pursue the team’s direction unless we have a clear reason not to go there.” The review list holds it as a lean to confirm.
    • A5, a special type, as ZZ32Vector is.
  • Decision B: where unboxed arithmetic happens. The ways on file: Java helpers over whole arrays; generated code that holds double locals and emits dadd and dmul wherever the checker’s type is RR64; or both. The plan puts it in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.
  • Decision D: the sizes in the model’s own types. A diff on file gives the flat program’s arrays sized types, 21 model lines out and 29 in. It comes to you as a diff.
  • The element width: RR64 as the model is written, or RR32. The default is RR64.

Your decision asks for the whole preparation before the switch-over, and only the work after. The coordinator reads the preparation as plain explainers of these decisions, such as this page. That reading waits for your review too.

Arrays in Fortress

You asked how arrays work, how the rehearsal ran them with no array decision taken, and what work stands before an array program runs. This page goes from small programs up to the design. Each program on it ran under walk today, and its output is shown as it printed.

1The short answers

  • The array program that runs first is the rehearsal’s smallest one. It makes an array of 8 ZZ32 with the library’s factory, writes i i into each element, and prints a[5] = 25. After the second run of the batch that is landing now, it compiles against the one library, the interpreter’s library. It runs only in the batch after that, once the whole library compiles to bytecode.
  • You need to do nothing now. The rehearsal ran arrays with no array decision, because an array is library code: Fortress traits and objects over a store, the object that holds the elements. The compiler compiles them as it compiles any other library code. The open array decisions are about speed and about the model’s own types. They aren’t about running.
  • An array is half language, half library. The language gives the literal [1 2 3], the type shorthand ZZ32[3] and the subscript syntax. The library gives every type behind them. Array1, Vector and Matrix are in FortressLibrary, which every program sees without an import.

3The syntax is the language’s, the types are the library’s

You were right twice. The literal looks built in, and it is. The types are library types, and they are too. Here is the split.

The language, its parser and walk, give:

  • the literal, [1 2 3; 4 5 6];
  • the shorthand T[n, m] for Array2[\T, 0, n, 0, m\];
  • the subscript forms a[i], a[i, j] and a[i] := v;
  • the static parameters, [\T, nat n\], where nat marks a size that the type carries.

The library gives:

  • Array[\E, I\], an array of any rank with no size in its type. I is the index type: ZZ32, or a pair (ZZ32, ZZ32) for rank 2.
  • Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\], Array2 and Array3, with a lowest index and a size for each dimension.
  • Vector[\T, nat s0\] and Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\], for numbers only, with their arithmetic.
  • the factories: array1[\T, n\](), vector, matrix, and array[\T\](n) for a size known only when the program runs.
  • the subscript itself. a[i] calls a library operator, opr[i:I]:E = get(offset(i)), as Swift’s a[i] calls a subscript that the type declares.

The two meet at two names. Walk knows the trait Array plus the rank, and the factory __builtinFactory plus the rank. To build [1 2 3] at a declared type, walk calls __builtinFactory1[\ZZ32, 0, 3\]() and copies the elements in. The library’s comment says the names are “enshrined” in walk. A literal with no declared type is not built into an array today.

So Array1 is not in a collections component that a program imports, as List is. It’s in FortressLibrary, the prelude of the one library. The specification notes that the library provides Array1 to Array3.

In your frames: Swift’s [Double] is shorthand for the standard library’s Array<Double>. Fortress’s RR64[3] is shorthand for the library’s Array1[\RR64,0,3\], and the size is part of the type. Scala’s Array[Double] is a special case of the Scala compiler, which makes it a JVM double[]. Fortress has no such special case yet. Which store an element type gets is one of your open questions.

4How the sizes ride in the type

The library’s rank-1 array keeps no length field. It reads its size from its type:

trait ReadableArray1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\] ...
    getter size(): ZZ32 = s0
    opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0
    offset(i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
        r = i - b0
        if NOT (0 <= r < s0) then oops(1, b0, s0, i) end
        r
    end

|a| is s0, and the bounds check compares the index with s0. A product names a shared size once, so the shapes must match:

opr juxtaposition[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat n, nat m\]
    (me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], v: Vector[\T,m\]): Vector[\T,n\]

An n-by-m matrix times a vector of m gives a vector of n. Here is a program that uses the sizes, with a 2-by-2 matrix to show that order matters:

  w: RR64[4] = [1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0]
  println("len(u) = " len(u) ", len(w) = " len(w))
  q: RR64[2,2] = [1.0 2.0; 3.0 4.0]
  x: RR64[2] = [1.0 1.0]
  println("q x = " (q x) ", x q = " (x q))
  m: RR64[2,3] = [1.0 0.0 2.0; 0.0 1.0 1.0]
  println("m u = " (m u))
  println("u + u = " (u + u))
  println("u + w = " (u + w))
end

m u = [0#2][ 7.0 5.0 ]

How each path carries the sizes:

  • Walk keeps them in each object’s type when the program runs: __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\], the library’s vector object at size 3. When walk makes the object, it binds each nat parameter to its number, so a body reads s0 as a value. Walk finds a mismatch only when the line runs.
  • The compiled checker checks sizes before the compile, so it refuses a call whose sizes don’t match. Two sizes are equal when they’re written alike once numerals are computed: 2 3 equals 6, but m n doesn’t equal n m. It refuses a size outside ZZ32’s range, to match the JVM’s int indices.
  • The compiled run time compiles a generic declaration once, as a template. At first use, the class loader makes the class of each instance, and the sizes become part of its name. The rehearsal’s stack trace names __DefaultMatrix⟦FRR64,3,4⟧. Inside, each size has one descriptor object, from RTTIsize.of, used in type tests when the program runs. Where a body reads s0 as a number, the loader writes in the constant, FZZ32.make(3). This is your picture of sizes stamped into a class, as Swift mangles names. No optimization reads a size yet: a loop bounded by the size constant measured no faster than one bounded by the length read when it runs.

A size known only when the program runs comes through reflect:

make(n: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.5)

x = make(2 + 1)
println("x = " x)
typecase x of
  Vector[\RR64,3\] => println("x is a Vector[\\RR64,3\\] when it runs")
  else => println("x has no size when it runs")
end
x = [0#3][ 0.5 0.5 0.5 ]
x is a Vector[\RR64,3\] when it runs

The declared type Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] holds no size. Inside the factory, reflect(n) turns the number into a value N[\3\] that carries it, and a generic function that takes N[\n\] binds n to 3 for that call. So the object is a sized vector when it runs. The checker reads such a size as fixed for that one call. A compiled call of this kind fails the JVM’s verification today, so it runs only under walk. microGPT’s flat program makes its arrays this way, with types that hold no size.

5Where the elements live today

A Vector[\RR64,3\] made by array1 is three objects deep:

  1. __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\], the vector, holds mem: PrimitiveArray[\RR64,3\];
  2. PrimitiveArray holds mem: JavaArrayStore, the store;
  3. the store holds the elements in Java.

A matrix of 2 by 3 holds one rank-1 store of s0 s1 cells, 6, row by row, and reads cell i s1 + j. A size can be a product.

The third object differs by path:

  • Under walk, walk answers the store with its own Java object, an AtomicArray of walk’s boxed values.
  • On the compiled path, against the one library, as in the rehearsal, the store is the Java class FortressArrayStore, an Object[] of boxed values such as FRR64 objects. Inside an atomic block, each read and write of an element goes through the transaction, keyed by the array and the index.
  • On the compiled path on main today, there is no array type at all: the compiler’s prelude has none, so a program that names Array1 gets “Array1 is undefined”.

The store over a bare double array is PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\], the team’s immutable RR64 array, in the one library’s NativeArray. Its store is a JavaRR64ArrayStore. Walk answers it with a double[], and its compiled class, FortressRR64ArrayStore, holds a double[]. It has get and init, and no put, since it’s immutable. “Nothing chooses it” means this:

  PrimImmutableRR64Array[\3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the double[] store")
  PrimImmutableArray[\RR64,3\] => println("immutableArray1 chose the general store")
  else => println("immutableArray1 chose something else")
end

r.init0(0, 1.5)
r.init0(1, 2.5)
r.init0(2, 0.25)
println("the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = " (r[0] + r[1] + r[2]))
immutableArray1 chose the general store
the double[] store, named by hand: r[0] + r[1] + r[2] = 4.25

The store works, but the factory for an immutable RR64 array returns the general store. How a factory chooses each element type’s store is your first open question.

The native arrays of the compiler’s prelude are something else. The prelude is the compiled path’s own small library, which goes at the switch-over. It has ZZ32Vector, over a Java int[] in the class FZZ32Vector, and StringVector, over a String[], both written by hand by the team in August 2011. They have no type parameters and no size in their types. There’s no RR64 version. Neither is a generator, so for x <- v fails, and neither can be a type argument. Each read takes a boxed index and returns a new boxed ZZ32: the storage is unboxed, and the traffic is boxed. Your decision keeps the prelude as it is and deletes its files at the switch-over, so these two go with it.

6Boxing, and what it costs

A boxed number is a number held in a heap object. On the compiled path an RR64 is an object of the Java class FRR64, with one double field: Java’s Double against double, or a Double[] against a double[]. An unboxed number is the bare double, in a register or in a double[]. Today the code generator boxes every number, so a compiled RR64 loop holds no dadd or dmul.

What it costs, measured in Java models of the compiled run time’s boxes against double[]:

  • a dot product over 4K elements: 6.3 times;
  • a 16 by 16 matrix product: 6.5 times;
  • the row lift, a function applied to each row: 2.6 times.

An Object[] behind an interface, with a cast on each read, added only 9 %, 1.6 % and 4.8 % on top. The boxes cost, the generic container doesn’t.

The JIT, HotSpot’s C2, removes a temporary box in a hot loop when the box doesn’t escape. One box stays for each assignment to a mutable variable in each iteration, 24 bytes for an RR64. That was observed once. An array element escapes, since it’s stored, so its box stays.

A double[] store alone buys nothing while each read still makes a box. In the Java model, a dot product over a double[] read and written through a boxing accessor ran at 8.9 times the bare loop, against 6.4 times for boxed storage. So storage and traffic are two problems. Where the elements live is the store’s question. Where the reads and the arithmetic run unboxed is a separate decision.

“We go with boxed numbers now” means this. Your decision makes each built-in number type one value object, so that compiled code can later hold a ZZ32 as a bare int. The second run’s number rung writes each number type’s class over a small hand-written class that holds the bare value. Code still passes boxes until the unboxing decision is built, in the phase in which microGPT runs fast.

For arrays it changes no decision. Your decision already fixes the goal: each number type’s array stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and the sizes in the types now, not first as run-time fields. Your words of 8 November: “All numerical code in HPC settings must eventually run unboxed in the compiled path. All arrays must have the most efficient and performant implementation possible. Otherwise it will remain a research toy, not an HPC language.” The store in a field is the seam: a factory can later put a double[] store under Vector[\RR64,n\] without changing the traits or a program.

Probe Y, on 13 November, ran the same programs in one build that serves either library by one setting. The batch now landing puts that setting on main: FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one makes the compile command read the one library.

The dot program, as rewritten from the rehearsal’s description:

a: Array1[\RR64,0,1000\] = array1[\RR64,1000\]()
b: Array1[\RR64,0,1000\] = array1[\RR64,1000\]()
for i <- seq(0#1000) do
  a[i] := asFloat(i)
  b[i] := 1.0
end

println("dot = " || s.asString)

Under walk today, it and the array program printed the compiled runs’ lines, dot = 499500.0 and a[5] = 25.

The rehearsal timed that loop run 5K times, 5M iterations. Compiled, the whole process took 1.4 s, about 0.8 s for the loop. Under walk, 39.8 s, about 36 s for the loop. Java over double[] takes 7.5 ms in a cold JVM and 4.4 ms warm. So it’s about 160 ns an iteration against about 1 ns, of the order of 100 times. That’s one run each, in different sessions at different loads, with the JIT’s warm-up inside the 0.8 s and the JVM’s verifier off. It’s an order of magnitude, no more.

Why so slow, if boxing is 6 to 7 times? Boxing explains that much, by the Java models. The rest has no measured share. By reading the code, one read a[i] goes:

  1. to the subscript operator, which calls offset(i), with its bounds check against s0;
  2. to the vector’s get, then PrimitiveArray’s get, which casts the element to RR64 with a type test;
  3. to the store’s get, through a generated wrapper, to a Java helper;
  4. to FortressArrayStore.get, which checks whether the thread runs a transaction, then reads the element as a volatile read, as for a variable that another thread may write.

The record names four suspects for the rest:

  • those layers of the read, with their checks and the cast;
  • the range seq(0#1000), which calls a closure for each iteration;
  • the check for a transaction before every read and write of the mutable s, outside atomic too, 1 to 2 ns a check, which another probe measured at 64 % of a loop over an array with mutable variables;
  • the new box for s in each iteration.

Read the number as you’d read a timing from a Swift debug build. It shows that the code runs, and how far it is from the goal. It doesn’t show what the code will cost. A profile that splits the time is proposed in the plan, not run.
